data.title: Why London-Los Angeles Flights Curve Over Greenland Instead Of Flying Straight West
data.incipit: Published Sep 19, 2026, 3:00 PM EDT Daniel comes to Simple Flying with a business focused approach to the aviation world. Daniel...
data.body: Published Sep 19, 2026, 3:00 PM EDT Daniel comes to Simple Flying with a business focused approach to the aviation world. Daniel enjoys analyzing strategy and how companies move against each other to gain a step ahead in the skies. Besides strategy, Daniel also has a passion for aircraft design and the history of aviation. Based in New York The most direct route between London and Los Angeles takes an aircraft over northern Ireland, southern Greenland, Hudson Bay in Canada, and the Rocky Mountains before finally arriving in LA. You might think that it would just be a straight line, but this isn't the case because the Earth is curved. The Mercator projection that you often see depicts great circle routes as curved, but on a globe, these same routes reveal themselves as true straight lines. However, flight planning is more complicated than just drawing a straight line. Flight dispatchers create routes for each specific flight, and you often find deviations every day. This is because factors like weather and winds can significantly change what is economical for the carrier to operate. Airlines aim to reduce operating costs where possible, which means cutting down on fuel burn and flying the most efficient route, which isn't always a straight line. Even factors like overflight fees can play a major role, and dispatchers also need to take into account operational constraints. Winds Over The Atlantic Ocean Credit: JW.photography31 I Shutterstock A weather phenomenon that occurs over the North Atlantic is the polar jet stream. These fast-moving winds are located in the upper atmosphere where airliners fly, and traveling in them can significantly cut flight times due to their intensity. However, these winds flow eastwards over the North Atlantic, which means that flights from the US to Europe usually fly with a tailwind. Aircraft traveling from Europe to the US, meanwhile, face a headwind, which means that they need to be routed around the jet stream. Typically, the airliners headed west will take a route closer to the great circle route over the ocean compared to eastbound flights, as they're actively avoiding the jet stream instead of trying to catch the wind. However, this isn't always the case because the location, direction, and intensity of the jet stream change. In addition, flights need to route around severe weather as well. As such, exact routes vary depending on the day for transatlantic flights, although they usually correspond similarly to a true straight line. The northern polar jet stream flows across the North Atlantic, Europe, Asia, the North Pacific, and North America . In addition, the polar jet stream exists in the Southern Hemisphere, mainly wrapping around Antarctica, while there are also two weaker subtropical jet streams located closer to the Equator. While jet streams exist throughout the world, the North Atlantic polar jet stream is arguably the most impactful due to the high volume of flights traveling through this corridor and the strength of the winds here. The North Atlantic Tracks Credit: Sergey Kustov I Shutterstock The polar jet stream over the North Atlantic is strongest in a relatively small corridor, which concentrates flights together. What's more, there is no radar over the ocean, resulting in an area dense with flights that can't be monitored by radar. To maintain safety, separation requirements are increased over the ocean, and for further organization, flights operate within multiple designated flight routes, dubbed the 'North Atlantic Tracks'. This further keeps flights away from their great circle route. The tracks are used for aircraft traveling between flight levels 290 and 410 inclusive, and each set of tracks is published every day by Gander Centre and Shanwick Centre . Flight dispatchers plan routes in advance of the tracks being published and send route preferences to Gander/Shanwick, which are usually granted. Because of how the tracks are developed, planes don't always fly in straight lines from one end of the ocean to the other, and they often deviate away from a great circle route. The tracks are primarily used for flights between Europe and the US East Coast, meaning that many flights to the US West Coast often fly north of the tracks. If winds favor a more southerly route, however, the flight may be routed via the tracks, which takes it off its great circle route but saves time overall because the aircraft travels at a higher ground speed. However, this mainly applies to eastbound flights, and less so to westbound flights that usually aim to fly north of the jet stream. Taking Overflight Fees Into Consideration Credit: Karolis Kavolelis I Shutterstock It's hardly something that comes to mind for those onboard the aircraft, but an operator (the airline flying the aircraft) is required to pay fees to certain foreign countries that its planes overfly during a given flight. These fees are set by the country, and they can even vary by which part of the country the aircraft operates over. For flights between Europe and North America, most aircraft have to overfly Canada , and the country is notorious for charging extremely high overflight fees. For the most part, airlines simply have to pay the amount because there isn't any way to fly around Canada on these routes. However, when wind conditions permit, airlines may schedule routes to fly over US airspace or enter oceanic airspace earlier to pay less in Canadian overflight fees. This often adds time to the flight and can even increase the fuel cost for the flight, but the equation works out if the added flight time isn't dramatic and the reduction in overflight fee costs offsets the added fuel burn. Canada isn't the only country that charges high overflight fees due to its location . However, it is the most relevant nation when discussing transatlantic routes. It's another example of the complexities of planning flights, especially long-haul services. Airlines are hyperfocused on keeping costs low, but there are also a huge number of factors that can influence a given flight's route. Accounting for these factors is why planes fly different routes essentially every day, and why it's uncommon for a flight to simply go in a straight line. An Airline's Goal When Planning Flights Credit: MC MEDIASTUDIO I Shutterstock It doesn't make much of a difference to the airline how long a flight takes. Airlines simply always fly their aircraft at their most fuel-efficient speed, and while dispatchers do aim to route flights through favorable tailwinds while avoiding headwinds, this is to cut down on fuel cost first. If it's more favorable to take the long way around Canada and pay less in overflight fees, then the airline will do that even if the flight gets extended, depending on wind conditions and just how significant the detour is. While it's easy to compare the ground distance traveled with great circle distance, these numbers are somewhat meaningless to the airline. Track Name Meaning Minimum Distance Track Calculates the shortest distance between two points Minimum Time Track Calculates the route with the lowest flight time Minimum Fuel Track Calculates the route with the lowest fuel burn Minimum Cost Track Calculates the route with the lowest overall cost, taking into account all factors Airline dispatchers usually can calculate a minimum distance route, but this doesn't account for factors like weather, making it an irrelevant figure in most cases. Dispatchers can also calculate routes with the least amount of time and the least amount of fuel burn, which are usually fairly similar. However, it's the lowest-cost option that's most relevant and usually ends up being selected . The fuel burn track can be informative to dispatchers, as can the lowest time and lowest distance figures. However, the cost figure takes into account fuel burn, as well as overflight charges, possible missed curfew costs, crew costs, and more. Given the importance of keeping operating costs low and just how many variables are in play when planning long-haul services, this is by far the most common track that dispatchers plan for flight routes. If the flight happens to be shorter, then that's an extra benefit. The Most Extreme Examples Credit: The Global Guy I Shutterstock North America and the North Atlantic are fairly open regions, but across the ocean, there are significant airspace closures in the Middle East and Russia. Russian airspace in particular had become crucial for flights between Europe and Asia, but the shutdown of the airspace meant that many airlines now needed to route around the massive country. Most flights now travel south of Russia, but some head north near the Arctic and follow the Russian coastline . Meanwhile, certain flights between Japan and the UK cross the Pacific, traverse North America, and fly over the Atlantic instead. Elsewhere, Singapore Airlines operates the world's two longest nonstop flights, from Singapore to New York JFK and Newark Airport. A great circle route would see the flight fly near the North Pole, but because of the jet stream, the departing flight travels over the Pacific and Canada instead. Meanwhile, the returning flight occasionally mirrors this route, but more often will fly over the Atlantic, Europe, and South Asia, catching tailwinds from the jet stream. Both of these routes traverse much longer distances, but take less time than a straight-line route because of winds. Qantas is planning to begin flying from Sydney to JFK and London in 2027 as part of Project Sunrise. A great circle route for the Sydney services would see the aircraft fly westbound through the Middle East, but the airline has softly revealed that some flights between Sydney and London specifically (not the return) will fly over the North Pacific and the Atlantic, once again because of tailwinds.

data.title: US regulator opens inquiry into Anthropic, OpenAI and other AI labs
data.incipit: The US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has begun a broad investigation into AI developers, including Anthropic and OpenAI, to assess the risks their technologies may pose to consumers, reported Reuters citing...
data.body: The US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has begun a broad investigation into AI developers, including Anthropic and OpenAI, to assess the risks their technologies may pose to consumers, reported Reuters citing a senior FTC official. The move represents the first official US enforcement action targeting potentially hazardous AI agents, following July incidents that raised concerns over unregulated systems. As part of the inquiry, the FTC plans to issue formal requests for information and require testimony from executives at leading AI companies, including Anthropic, OpenAI, and the research group METR. Anthropic and OpenAI have previously used METR to conduct independent reviews of security issues related to their agentic AI applications. The investigation received further impetus after AI agents developed by OpenAI were found to have breached the open-source platform Hugging Face. According to the FTC official, the agents explored the AI coding hub in search of vulnerabilities before launching a large-scale attack, accelerating the Commission's review. FTC chairman Andrew Ferguson had already expressed concerns about major AI companies prior to the Hugging Face incident. In an interview with Reuters last week, Ferguson indicated that developers who direct AI agents to conduct cybersecurity testing that results in hacks could be held liable for the resulting damages. "The US should look to existing laws before seeking to pass new ones regulating AI," Ferguson stated at the Reuters Momentum AI event in Austin. The FTC has general authority to take enforcement action against companies for unfair or deceptive practices, including insufficient measures to guard consumers' data. The Commission has exercised this power in prior data security cases. Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump met with senior AI industry executives on 29 September. During the meeting, companies agreed to define voluntary standards. Trump has dismissed some concerns about AI as a "hoax" and emphasised maintaining the US's leadership in AI technology over pursuing new regulations. However, he has also said existing laws can hold AI companies accountable for harm caused by their products. "US regulator opens inquiry into Anthropic, OpenAI and other AI labs" was originally created and published by Verdict , a GlobalData owned brand.

data.title: Google’s AI model hacked three other companies during security breach
data.incipit: Google confirmed that its Gemini AI model inadvertently breached the computer systems of three real companies during a cybersecurity test conducted in May by security startup Irregular. The model accessed real-world corporate systems...
data.body: Google confirmed that its Gemini AI model inadvertently breached the computer systems of three real companies during a cybersecurity test conducted in May by security startup Irregular. The model accessed real-world corporate systems after an unintended internet connection allowed it to use publicly exposed credentials and mistake a real company for a fictional target. Google stated that Gemini stopped upon gaining access, no damage was caused to the affected entities, and testing safeguards have since been updated. The incident mirrors similar issues during security evaluations involving AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic interacting with real-world external systems. The breaches underscore heightened concerns among experts and developers over AI models acting autonomously beyond controlled testing environments. data.title: Ignite to promote Ghanaian shea butter on the global market — MyJoyOnline
data.incipit: Ignite Social Enterprise Limited in Ghana plans to promote Ghanaian shea butter on the international market through its digital platform. Regional consultant Paul Elikem Dovi announced this during the UPSA...
data.body: Ignite Social Enterprise Limited in Ghana plans to promote Ghanaian shea butter on the international market through its digital platform. Regional consultant Paul Elikem Dovi announced this during the UPSA 1000 & Ghana Entrepreneurship Conference in Accra, MyJoyOnline reports. Cooperation with manufacturers According to Dovi, Ignite Social Enterprise intends to cooperate with Ghanaian businesses, primarily companies in the agricultural and manufacturing sectors. Among the products the company plans to prioritize in its promotion efforts, he named shea butter and locally made watches. The company representative said this strategy is intended to expand Ignite's range of quality products and strengthen the competitiveness of Ghanaian brands on the international market. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram . Social e-commerce model Dovi noted that Ignite's mission is to make business ownership more accessible and help micro-entrepreneurs achieve financial independence. According to him, the platform operates under a people-oriented social e-commerce model. He explained that the platform offers selected products for a healthy lifestyle and everyday use, as well as digital tools, training and an artificial intelligence-based educational platform. Ignite Social Enterprise was the main sponsor of the five-day conference, which began on Monday, September 14, at the Kofi Ohene-Kondu Auditorium of the University of Professional Studies, Accra. The event brought together young entrepreneurs, business leaders and industry experts; the company urged Ghana's youth to create affordable and sustainable businesses that benefit communities. data.title: This is the data centre capital of the world. They’re starting to regret it
data.incipit: Loudoun County, Virginia: When plans first dropped for a big new data centre next to Lindsay Shaw’s home in Sterling, Virginia, she welcomed it. “It is what it is,” she thought at the time. “We’re in the data...
data.body: Loudoun County, Virginia: When plans first dropped for a big new data centre next to Lindsay Shaw’s home in Sterling, Virginia, she welcomed it. “It is what it is,” she thought at the time. “We’re in the data centre capital of the world.” What she didn’t know then was that this facility by Vantage Data Centres would not be connected to the electricity grid, and would be powered by its own gas turbines, at least for now. The resulting noise, which typically involves a high-pitched whistle sound, has become unbearable for many in the neighbourhood. Lindsay Shaw and partner Bob Salehi outside the Ashburn II Data Centre Campus, which is just metres from their home. Leigh Vogel for Sydney Morning Herald / The Age “It gets so loud some nights you can hear it over the TV in my house,” says Shaw, 38. “You can hear it over the air-conditioners, you can hear it over the lawnmower, you can hear it over anything else.” There are about 250 data centres operating or under construction in Loudoun County – the highest concentration anywhere in the world. Most were built between 2019 and 2014, but the spree has continued: in 2025, the county issued permits for more than 10 million square feet of data centre space. Drive along Waxpool Road or Loudoun County Parkway, and you will see the products of this boom: big boxes of largely windowless buildings with names like Equinix, QTS and H5, and dirt mounds surrounded by cranes. It is estimated that 70 per cent of global traffic passes through or is created in Loudoun County’s “data centre alley”. The Ashburn II Data Centre Campus looms over houses in Sterling, Virginia. Sydney Morning Herald But many of the county’s 450,000 residents – like Americans around the country – have had enough. On Tuesday night, dozens spoke at a public meeting to call for a pause on data centre approvals, which the board of county supervisors ultimately voted to support. A Loudoun resident for 20 years, Sarah Chen said: “I’ve watched it go from green pastures with livestock to feeling like livestock as our homes and health have been sold out to feed corporate greed. “We’ve built more than enough data centres in this county. Loudoun is infamous for them. We must have a full stop, and this moratorium is the beginning.” An Amazon data centre, part of data centre alley, in Ashburn, Virginia. Bloomberg Loudoun County alone has more data centres than Australia. That may change if state and federal governments forge ahead with plans to encourage AI development, while imposing rules and standards on where large AI data centres can be built and the power and water they consume. Whether Loudoun serves as a road map or a cautionary tale depends on who you talk to. This area of Virginia, just outside Washington DC, became a data centre powerhouse because of the dense fibre optic network built there in the 1990s, when AOL established a primary gateway in Loudoun County. The board of supervisors also granted by-right planning permission for data centres, allowing them to be built anywhere zoned for office development. Virginia’s state government maintains several financial incentives for data centres, reducing upfront costs and corporate income tax. County supervisor Juli Briskman says the true catalyst for the boom was the Great Recession of 2008-09, which arose from the US subprime mortgage crisis. “Communities were struggling with their tax base and tax revenue because of the dip in housing values,” she says. “The great folks at our economic development department realised, ‘Hey, we have this fibre in the ground, we have the infrastructure in place that we could start welcoming this newish industry.’ ” Economically, there is no doubt this has been a winner for Loudoun County – which is frequently cited as the wealthiest in America. Residents here enjoy very high household incomes, and the data centres raise $US1.2 billion ($1.68 billion) a year in tax revenue and climbing – accounting for 40 per cent of the county’s budget. Juli Briskman, who is on the Loudoun County Board of Supervisors, says the revenue is “wonderful” but residents have had enough. Michael Koziol That income subsidises increased services while enabling the county to reduce property taxes. It has cut real property taxes every year for the past 10 years, from $1.145 per $100 of assessed value to $0.805, saving homeowners thousands of dollars a year. “We’ve been able to almost eliminate the car tax, which is a hated tax in Virginia,” Briskman says. “We’ve been fully funding our excellent public school system, which is of course an economic driver.” She enumerates other benefits: a mental health facility built in two years, a $US22 million cheque to acquire and preserve Oak Hill, the historic estate of former president James Monroe. “There aren’t a lot of jurisdictions in the state where they could do that.” And yet Briskman, a Democrat, is leading the charge to crack down on data centres. “The revenue is wonderful, in large part,” she says. “But that’s just not an argument that’s holding water any more with our communities.” On a sunny weekday morning, Briskman takes this masthead on a walk around the off-grid Vantage data centre in Sterling, powered by its eight gas turbines. A low hum is audible out the front, but it’s when we go to the rear that the turbines’ high-pitched sound grows loud. This section abuts a business centre, not homes. Homes behind the Vantage Data Centre facility in Sterling, Virginia, which has the world’s highest concentration of data centres. There is a wall of backup diesel generators, which Lindsay Shaw says were supposed to be for emergencies but end up being used once or twice a month. “When you walk out you can taste the smoke, like walking into a pack of cigarettes,” she says. Shaw says neighbours’ children have developed respiratory illnesses that they attribute to the generators, and others have dry eye disease. “It’s been extremely negative, living next to it.” Vantage maintains that noise mitigation measures are in place and that independent assessments confirm the centre complies with sound targets. Last month, its vice president of public policy, Misty Allen, told a public meeting that the company had made several improvements to reduce noise, including wrapping sound blankets around the exterior, replacing vents with noise-suppressing hoods and attaching a demister and silencer on the exhaust fans. But the meeting was rattled when Allen revealed the facility is not expected to be connected to the power grid – and taken off the turbines – until 2040. “It is very much our intention and desire to connect to the Dominion grid as quickly as we possibly can when capacity becomes available,” she said. Briskman said the 2040 estimate created a problem for residents considering moving away from the area, who would now be unable to get a fair value for their homes. In a statement, Vantage said it was committed to continuous improvement and being a responsible long-term neighbour. “While the VA2 campus is in full compliance with applicable local noise ordinances, we know that isn’t enough given the concerns the community has expressed,” it said. “That is why we have been implementing additional noise mitigation measures based on community feedback, many of which have already been completed and are making a difference today.” Loudoun County had already removed the right for data centres to be built on land zoned for office use without explicit planning approval – a move matched by several Virginia counties. At Tuesday night’s meeting, the board of supervisors agreed to draft a resolution to pause new data centre applications for 12 months. It will go to a final vote next month. Opposition to data centres is rising across the United States. Here, a protester prepares to join a rally at the Missouri Capitol in Jefferson City. AP Photo/David A. Lieb Only one supervisor, Kristen Umstattd, opposed the pause. “I worry a little bit – maybe I worry a lot – about where we’re going as a board when we seem happy to ignore one area, one industry, that provides good-paying jobs,” said Umstattd, a Democrat who has been in local politics for four decades. “If we keep saying no – and we’ve begun to say no to these – and we shut down this industry, we’re going to lose the jobs that keep a thousand Loudoun families able to put food on their table. I just cannot get past that.” Representatives from local chambers of commerce made similar points at the meeting, saying a pause would send the wrong signal to businesses considering investments in Loudoun County. They also agreed Loudoun relied too heavily on data centre revenue and ought to diversify its economy. These battles are being fought around Virginia and the US. Harford County in Maryland, north of Baltimore, voted in June to permanently ban data centres. Woodford County in Kentucky passed a similar ban last week. Dozens of other counties, from North Carolina to Florida to New Mexico, have enacted temporary moratoriums or freezes on data centre permits. Local people complain of constant noise from nearby data centres. Sydney Morning Herald At a local level, the backlash against data centres – and anxiety about AI more broadly – is largely bipartisan. In Congress, too, many Republicans are joining Democrats in demanding AI regulations and a slowdown. A University of Massachusetts Amherst poll released last week found just 11 per cent of Americans – one in nine – said they would support the construction of a data centre in their local community. “The remarkable thing is that we can’t find a constituency that actually wants these data centres,” said Raymond La Raja, a professor of political science and co-director of the poll. Republicans were more receptive than Democrats, but they also opposed data centres. “Among the strongest MAGA supporters – the group most receptive to data centres – just 25 per cent support them being built nearby, compared with 42 per cent who oppose,” La Raja said. ‘I’m tired of being gaslit by being told it’s NIMBY ... We choose to live here, and we deserve a beautiful county where we don’t have to fear future development’. Sophia Chen, Loudoun County resident President Donald Trump is trying to change that. As the sector’s own leaders sound the alarm on unchecked AI development, he leapt to defend the industry and the data centres that enable it. “The only reason that communities throughout the USA should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” Trump wrote on Truth Social at the end of August. “If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame.” Days ago, Trump went further, labelling the anxiety a “hoax” perpetrated to advantage China, which he warned would leapfrog the US if development slowed down. “AI, and Data Centers, will be the Greatest Economic Development Engine in History ­­– Bigger than Oil, Gold, Diamonds, or even the Internet. It will not be stopped by brilliantly run Destructive Forces during the Term of President DONALD J. TRUMP!” Much of Trump’s thinking on the topic is informed by entrepreneur and investor David Sacks, the president’s former AI tsar who now serves as co-chair of the President’s Council of Advisers on Science and Technology. Sacks told Politico’s Decoded Summit in Washington on Wednesday that the current panic about AI was being driven by the media and politically vested interests ahead of the midterm election on November 3. “We already have a lot of laws and regulations that pertain to AI,” he said, referring to rules on cyberattacks, privacy violations and product liability. “We can have an intelligent conversation about [whether] we need something else on top of that. But it’s hard to have that conversation when you have this fearmongering going on.” In Loudoun County, however, it is not fear – it’s the reality of life in the world’s data centre capital, as residents clamour for an off-switch. “I’m tired of being gaslit by being told it’s NIMBY – not in my backyard – to protest data centres or substations or power lines because they’re ugly,” said resident Sophia Chen. “Don’t tell us looks aren’t important – they are. We choose to live here, and we deserve a beautiful county where we don’t have to fear future development.” Juli Briskman says governments and communities in Australia contemplating a future with more data centres should not automatically say no, but they ought to be strategic. “It’s a great source of revenue,” she says. “You just need to be smart about where you put them, about the environmental impacts, about the electrical infrastructure that’s required. You need to have the full picture, which we didn’t always have.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world. Sign up for our weekly What in the World newsletter .

data.title: Hyatt hotels, business class: Inside the 24-hour economy commissioner’s nine overseas trips
data.incipit: September 20, 2026 — 5:00amThe state’s 24-hour economy commissioner has made nine overseas trips investigating nightlife abroad since February 2024, with his role and these expenses now under parliamentary...
data.body: September 20, 2026 — 5:00am The state’s 24-hour economy commissioner has made nine overseas trips investigating nightlife abroad since February 2024, with his role and these expenses now under parliamentary scrutiny amid wider cuts across the arts sector. Madrid, London, Hong Kong, Beijing, Amsterdam, Singapore, Barcelona and San Francisco are among the cities NSW 24-Hour Commissioner Michael Rodrigues has visited, staying in boutique hotels and flying premium economy or business class. Michael Rodrigues, NSW’s first 24-hour economy commissioner, in Burwood. James Brickwood Logged expenditure, accessed via a standing order and obtained by this masthead, reveals Rodrigues travelled between Europe, the US and Asia multiple times over the two years, meeting with overseas counterparts and attending multiple venues and networking events. Critics have blasted Rodrigues’ trips, noting they were undertaken as the 62-year-old Australian Design Centre was forced to close due to a lack of government funding , and a parliamentary inquiry found that the push to revive Sydney’s night-time reputation has come at direct cost to the state’s arts and culture sectors. Details of the commissioner’s travel spending have emerged following this masthead’s reporting on a pre-operational spending spree at the billion-dollar Powerhouse Parramatta . The Powerhouse and the Office of the 24-Hour Economy Commissioner are in NSW Arts and Night-time Economy Minister John Graham’s remit. Rodrigues was appointed to the newly established role in 2021 as the state’s first 24-hour economy commissioner to improve Sydney’s night-time economy. A spokesperson for the NSW Department of Creative Industries said his role included raising Sydney and NSW’s international profiles, strengthening our reputation as a vibrant global destination, and attracting investment and tourism. Graham said the commissioner’s overseas travel helped restore Sydney’s reputation among global “thought leaders” at some of the most “influential policy forums”. “An important part of the commissioner’s work has involved rebuilding our reputation overseas after the lockout era damaged the global reputation of Sydney,” Graham said. On a three-day trip to Barcelona in January and February 2025, Rodrigues met his Spanish night-time commissioner counterpart for “both cities to exchange insights and share experiences in addressing challenges associated with nighttime governance”. Rodrigues spent the first day in the Spanish city with Barcelona-based Venezuelan night-time governance consultant Andreina Seijas and went to a private event featuring Italian artist Davide Quayola. This was followed by dinner at Xeixa, a restaurant specialising in Catalan cuisine inside a former brothel that inspired one of Picasso’s works, then the historic Dr Stravinsky cocktail bar. The second Barcelona day’s morning involved informal and formal discussions with the city’s night office, followed by lunch at the city’s oldest restaurant, Can Culleretes. Rodrigues then took an “institutional photograph” that included Graham, who paid for his own trip while on work leave. Next, the commissioner visited Barcelona’s beachfront clubs and bars with other representatives, later explored the historic theatre district, including three venues (Sala Apolo, El Molino and La Paloma), had dinner to discuss the “challenges and opportunities in the local scene”, and ended the day with a club visit to Razzmatazz. Here, Rodrigues stayed until 1am to observe “its transition from a concert venue to a mega-club” as well as review its “weekend operational strategy ... [and how] neighbouring venues and local police manage safety in response to rising noise complaints”, according to a document titled “lessons learned” following the trip. The commissioner’s third and final day in Barcelona began at historic Catalan cafe Els Quatre Gats, where Picasso held his first-ever solo exhibition before heading to the Time Out Market. Rodrigues capped off the day by walking along the Consell de Cent Superblock and visiting three bars, including Sips, which was ranked third in the world at the time. Some of Rodrigues’ learnings from Barcelona included comparing each city’s Olympic legacy, the need for Sydney to adopt a decentralised approach, and the importance of public-private collaboration and nocturnal heritage. The NSW arts minister (centre-left) and the 24-Hour commissioner (right) in Barcelona. The minister was there on work leave and paid for the trip himself. Standing order document “During the 19th century, the people of Barcelona began experiencing the proliferation of new forms of life, leisure and social interaction, laying the foundation for its night-time economy,” his reflections noted. “Establishments such as Bar Marsella (est. 1820), Els Quatre Gats (est. 1896) and London Bar (est. 1910) have historically served as meeting points for intellectuals, artists, workers and unionists, with frequent visitors including Picasso, Dali and Ernest Hemingway. “The tangible and intangible value of these establishments highlights the importance of implementing mechanisms to protect them from disappearing and to preserve their cultural significance.” In a statement to this masthead, Rodrigues said his travelling was part of “international engagement, [which] is an important part of ensuring NSW remains competitive globally”. “My focus is ensuring that all international engagement delivers value for NSW businesses and communities and continues to drive the growth and success of the 24-hour economy in our state,” he said. NSW Greens MP Cate Faehrmann said she made the travel inquiries following industry concern that the 24-hour economy commissioner had a significant and growing budget, at a time of cuts in other areas of the arts budget, with “not a lot to show for it”. “It must be particularly galling for struggling artists and musos to see money that is supposed to be revitalising this state’s arts and cultural sectors being spent on business-class flights and posh hotels,” Faehrmann said. “The closing of the Australian Design Centre should never have been allowed to happen on this government’s watch, but clearly its priorities lie elsewhere.” Rodrigues’ Barcelona trip, where he stayed at four-star hotel Casa Bonay for about $350 a night, was part of a larger trip to Europe that included London, Amsterdam and Birmingham. That trip alone cost roughly $10,000 in flights and accommodation. He stayed at the $500-a-night Hoxton Shoreditch in London, the $600-a-night Hotel V Nesplein in Amsterdam and the more budget-friendly Hyatt Regency in Birmingham, which is about $200 per night. In March, when the commissioner travelled to China and Hong Kong for a NSW Creative Industries multi-day event, he flew from Sydney in business class and premium economy. Meanwhile, Amelia Rowe, a screen investment manager at Screen NSW, flew premium economy to the same event. All up, the commissioner’s travel from February 2024 until March 2026 exceeds $80,000, including flights, accommodation, meals and incidentals. But the 24-Hour Office said Rodrigues’ most expensive trip was funded by non-profit organisation Aspen Institute, costing roughly $16,800 for a trip to Madrid in April 2026 to speak at Bloomberg’s CityLab conference on urban planning ideas. Meanwhile, Singapore’s National Development Office covered the commissioner’s accommodation and transport between the hotel and airport for the World Cities Summit in June 2026. Rodrigues’ travel expenses to San Francisco in October 2025 to attend the World Economic Forum are yet to be formally reported. “All other travel has been funded in accordance with existing departmental travel and financial policies,” a spokesperson for the Department of Creative Industries, Tourism, Hospitality and Sport, which houses the 24-Hour Office, said. During budget estimates in August, committee chair Faehrmann asked Rodrigues about the travel. “I was invited to speak in the UK and I took that opportunity to go to Barcelona, partly because it’s one of the comparable cities that the Committee for Sydney had identified that we should look at,” he said. “Temperate environment, coastal, as opposed to other international cities that we sometimes draw comparison to.” In his statement, Rodrigues said international travel was part of the government’s 24-Hour Economy Strategy. “The 24-hour economy ... [is] a growing, $110 billion sector that supports more than 1.27 million jobs across NSW,” he said. “Increasingly, NSW is being asked to share our industry-leading expertise on precinct management, cultural activation and night-time economy policy with other jurisdictions in Australia and overseas, establishing NSW’s reputation as a tourism destination of first choice.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. data.title: Nigerian Agency NMDPRA Claims It Doesn't Fix Petrol Prices As Nigerians Groan Under Rising Costs
data.incipit: The Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA) has clarified that it does not determine or fix the pump price of Premium Motor Spirit (PMS), commonly known as petrol, under the Petroleum Industry Act (PIA) 2021. The clarification comes amid growing concerns and hardship being experienced by Nigerians following the recent increase in the retail prices of petrol across the country.
data.body: The clarification comes amid growing concerns and hardship being experienced by Nigerians following the recent increase in the retail prices of petrol across the country. The Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA) has clarified that it does not determine or fix the pump price of Premium Motor Spirit (PMS), commonly known as petrol, under the Petroleum Industry Act (PIA) 2021. The clarification comes amid growing concerns and hardship being experienced by Nigerians following the recent increase in the retail prices of petrol across the country. In a statement signed by its management, the NMDPRA acknowledged the financial pressure caused by the rising pump prices, noting that the situation is placing additional burdens on households, transport workers and businesses. The Authority said it was “fully sensitive” to the difficulties being faced by Nigerians and remained committed to ensuring that relief becomes possible as market conditions stabilise. According to the NMDPRA, the legal framework governing the downstream petroleum sector does not empower it to arbitrarily set petrol pump prices under the current deregulated market. The Authority said Section 205(1) of the Petroleum Industry Act provides that wholesale and retail prices of petroleum products shall be based on unrestricted free-market pricing conditions. It added that under the provision, the NMDPRA does not fix pump prices or issue administrative price templates for petroleum products. The Authority further explained that Sections 205(2) to 205(4) of the PIA restrict government intervention in petroleum pricing to exceptional circumstances where there is formal evidence of a declared market failure. It said no such market failure has been declared. The NMDPRA, however, stressed that deregulation does not mean petroleum marketers and other industry operators are free to engage in practices that violate competition and consumer protection laws. It cited Section 216 of the PIA, which empowers the Authority to prevent anti-competitive practices, price-fixing and abuse of market dominance within the petroleum industry. The regulator also disclosed that it is intensifying efforts to protect the stability of petroleum supply and prevent illegal diversion of products out of the country. It said it is conducting a joint security operation with the Nigeria Customs Service (NCS) and other relevant security agencies to increase surveillance along border corridors and tackle the smuggling of petroleum products. The NMDPRA also said it was working with the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC) to monitor the market and protect consumers from exploitative practices. According to the authority, both agencies have a formal Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) under which they conduct joint surveillance of the petroleum market. The surveillance, it said, is aimed at detecting and addressing practices including price-gouging, collusion, under-dispensing of petroleum products and the sale of products whose quality has been compromised. The authority said it is also opening dedicated feedback and reporting channels through which members of the public and industry stakeholders can report suspected irregular pricing and other exploitative trade practices. It said such reports would be subjected to immediate regulatory investigation and enforcement where violations are established. The NMDPRA reiterated that its statutory responsibility is to ensure energy security, promote fair competition and protect consumers while operating within the legal framework established by the Petroleum Industry Act. “The NMDPRA remains steadfast in fulfilling its statutory mandate to ensure energy security, foster fair competition, and protect consumers within the PIA's legal framework,” it added

data.body: About 90% of retirees may be making mistakes in how they use their savings by postponing spending from individual retirement accounts (IRAs) and 401(k) plans. MarketWatch reports this , citing a new Vanguard report. Accounts are being saved for later According to the publication, retirees may leave IRAs and 401(k)s untouched for a decade or longer. When they do eventually begin using these funds, they may spend them only to a limited extent. As MarketWatch notes, this approach may lead people to restrict their budgets at the start of retirement. As a result, some people die with more money than they had when they retired. data.body: Student Loans Borrowers who enroll in autopay will receive a 1% interest rate deduction on their student loans through June 30, 2028. WPVI Tuesday, September 29, 2026 2:59PM If you have college debt, now is the time to act to save some money. Borrowers who enroll in autopay can receive a 1% interest rate deduction on their federal student loans through June 30, 2028. But you must sign up by Wednesday to qualify for the discount. "Student loan borrowers should take advantage of every opportunity to reduce the cost of their loans," said Pennsylvania Attorney General Sunday. "Borrowers who are eligible for the one percent interest rate deduction should make sure they enroll now, and continue monitoring their accounts to ensure their payments and interest rate are being applied correctly." Top Stories The deduction applies to direct loans disbursed on or after July 1, 2012, including parent and graduate borrowers. Borrowers can enroll in autopay through their federal student loan servicer's website . If a borrower has already enrolled in autopay, they do not need to re-enroll. The interest rate deduction will automatically be applied to the account. Copyright © 2026 WPVI-TV. All Rights Reserved. Student Loans Watch Live Top Stories

data.title: Democrat Pete Buttigieg criticizes Trump's rollback of fuel-economy standards
data.incipit: Pete Buttigieg discusses Trump administration’s rollback of fuel efficiency standards ...
data.body: Pete Buttigieg discusses Trump administration’s rollback of fuel efficiency standards Download Embed < iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-5983537/nx-s1-9944251" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player"> Former U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg attends an NAACP fundraiser at Edisto Fork United Methodist Church on Aug. 22 in Orangeburg, S.C. Sean Rayford/Getty Images hide caption toggle caption Sean Rayford/Getty Images Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, a Democrat who served in the Biden administration, says the Trump administration's rollback of fuel-economy standards could leave drivers paying more over time and put U.S. automakers at a disadvantage globally. Speaking with NPR's Leila Fadel, Buttigieg challenged the administration's claim that the change will make vehicles more affordable. The Transportation Department says the new standards could cut the price of a new vehicle by about $1,300. But the administration also estimates drivers could pay about $1,600 more in fuel costs over the life of a vehicle — a figure Buttigieg argued does not fully account for higher gas prices or tariffs affecting the auto industry. The Corporate Average Fuel Economy, or CAFE, standards require carmakers to meet certain fuel-economy benchmarks as an average across their entire fleets. American automakers have broadly welcomed the rollback, saying the previous standards were out of step with consumer demand. But Buttigieg said the industry has historically resisted tougher fuel-economy rules before adapting to them. He also warned that weaker standards could slow U.S. auto innovation as China expands its electric vehicle industry and competes for a larger share of the global market. "Anything that means less innovation is going to help hand that advantage to China," Buttigieg said. Listen to the live interview by clicking the blue button above.
